summary:
Daegu stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The armed forces are the exception: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. Legal gender recognition is available, and on 8 May 2024 a court ruled that requiring sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity.

Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009, a week-long programme of parade and film events usually held in late June. Organisers ran the 2025 edition on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased', framing the event as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics. Court filings from the 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions show the same pattern: the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought injunctions against the festival and was dismissed each time.

State-adjacent restriction of the event is recurrent. Police again confined the 2025 march to a single bus-only lane, and in 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. In 2026 the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's own injunction request was cited as finding the police notice legitimate, on the reasoning that Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be kept clear for public welfare.

Organised counter-mobilisation is substantial and annual. In September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups maintain a standing 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu, and opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central street.

Opposition also works through formal complaints. On 8 June 2026 the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of festival venue, claiming the event risks infringing public welfare and reporting about 34,000 signatures. The petition answers the festival committee's January complaint against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation thus continued into the 2026 edition.

For a trans visitor, the practical picture is a visible but contested public presence: the festival proceeds, injunction bids fail in court each year, and no severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources. The surrounding conditions are not benign. South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report.
tangentialFactors:
Organised religious opposition in Daegu is more sustained and larger in scale than in Seoul, where established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive; a visitor comparing the two cities should expect a higher counter-protest presence around central Daegu during festival weeks.

National attitudes have shifted but remain divided: Pew Research Center recorded 18% of South Koreans saying homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013. Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society alongside its findings on LGBT discrimination.

The Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extending healthcare rights to same-sex partners, and the Supreme Court's acceptance of legal gender change for a transgender person with minor children, indicate a judiciary willing to recognise claims that the legislature has not. No same-sex marriage exists, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner.

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea remains a channel for complaints in principle, but in November 2023 it flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.
localsOnly:
Residents who organise or attend the festival carry the burden of the annual counter-mobilisation: roughly 3,500 counter-protesters from some 1,600 churches occupied a 450-metre stretch of central Daegu in September 2025, and an estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups maintain a permanent local objection committee. Merchants on Dongseong-ro are themselves party to the opposition, through the merchants' association's membership in the venue-change petition.

Local residents have no statutory anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, services or accommodation, since South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea accepts petitions but has issued no binding order in this dispute; its 34,000-signature venue petition was still an active filing as of June 2026.

Legal gender recognition is available nationally, including the 8 May 2024 ruling removing surgery as a precondition, and a Supreme Court allowance of gender change in the family relations register for a transgender person with minor children. Public restroom use has a documented, judicially enforced basis: on 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court held in a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights and awarded 300,000 won against the state.

Organisers have filed their own legal challenge to the policing regime, petitioning in January 2026 against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act, which governs assembly restrictions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a specific incident of violence or police mistreatment of a trans visitor in Daegu; the assessment that none is documented reflects absence of reporting, not a finding of safety.

The outcome of the June 2026 National Human Rights Commission of Korea venue petition is unresolved in these sources, as is any response to the festival committee's January 2026 complaint under Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.

Daegu-specific data on trans healthcare access, name-and-marker change processing at the local ward office, and gendered facilities in Daegu accommodation is not sourced here; the legal positions cited are national rulings applied locally.

The scale figures for the September 2025 counter-protest come from a sympathetic Korean Christian daily, and the 34,000-signature count for the venue petition is the petitioners' own claim; neither is independently verified in this inventory.
